blocks.text: Edwin Hubble laid the foundation of modern cosmology by showing that galaxies are moving away from the Earth and that their velocity increases with distance: the farther a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away.

blocks.title: Hubble's law
blocks.text: The recession velocity v of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance d from the Earth: v = Ho d (21.5), where Ho is Hubble's constant, about 2.3 x 10^-18 s^-1.

Fig 21.6 shows Hubble's law as a straight-line relation between the redshift (recession velocity) of galaxies and their distance from Earth; its slope is the Hubble constant, which measures the rate of cosmic expansion. All galaxies are moving away from each other, and an observer in another galaxy would see the same effect, because space itself is stretching. Scientists often use an inflated-balloon model (Fig 21.7): dots on the surface of a balloon represent galaxies and the skin represents space-time. As the balloon is inflated every dot 'sees' all the other dots moving away. So, wherever we are in the universe, we would see galaxies moving away: the expansion is happening everywhere and there is no special centre; Earth is not at the centre of the universe.

blocks.alt: Left: a graph of recession velocity against distance with dots scattered closely about a straight red line through the origin; v = Ho d, Ho about 2.3 x 10^-18 s^-1. Right: three balloons of increasing size, each with four dots on it, showing the dots further apart as the balloon inflates; every dot sees every other dot moving away and there is no centre.
blocks.caption: Hubble's law and the balloon model of the expanding universe (original diagram after Figs 21.6 and 21.7).
blocks.long_description: On a stretching balloon, dots that are twice as far apart separate twice as fast, which is exactly Hubble's law; no dot is the centre of the expansion.

blocks.text: Since the universe is expanding now, we can conceptually reverse time. This implies that (i) in the past the galaxies were closer together, and (ii) further back, all matter was compressed into a very small, dense and hot state. This idea is the basis of the Big Bang theory, which proposes that the universe began from an initial singularity about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since. Hubble's law provides strong observational evidence that the universe is not static but expanding, and is one of the key pillars of the Big Bang model. Fig 21.8 shows an approximate timeline of the universe from the Big Bang to the present.

blocks.alt: A narrow purple cone widening from left to right, with points along its axis: the Big Bang (0); recombination, when the first atoms formed and light could travel freely (380 thousand years); first stars appear (300 million years); early galaxies (1 billion years); and modern galaxies with accelerating expansion (today, about 13.8 billion years).
blocks.caption: Timeline of the universe (original diagram after Fig 21.8).
blocks.long_description: The widening cone stands for the size of the observable universe growing with time. Most of the history shown happened in the first billion years.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Before Hubble's discovery, most scientists thought the universe was static. Hubble's law turned that idea on its head, suggesting that the universe had a beginning and leading to the Big Bang theory.

Satellite remote sensing uses sensors aboard orbiting spacecraft to monitor and analyse Earth's environment from space. It lets scientists track deforestation, climate change, ocean temperatures and atmospheric composition. Unlike ground-based methods, it offers wide geographic coverage and repeated observations over time, making long-term environmental monitoring possible (Fig 21.9).

items: Source and illumination: the first element is a source that illuminates the target with electromagnetic radiation (usually the Sun).
Atmosphere: the radiation interacts with the atmosphere on its way, by scattering, reflection and so on.
Interaction with the target: the radiation interacts with the target; the interaction depends on the properties of the target and the radiation.
Recording with a sensor: the emitted or reflected radiation is recorded by a sensor that is remote (not in contact with the target).
Transmission and reception: the recorded data are transmitted to a receiving station and converted into a usable form such as images.
Interpretation and analysis: the processed image is interpreted, electronically or digitally, to obtain information.

blocks.alt: The Sun (1, source) sends radiation through the atmosphere (2) to the Earth (3, target); radiation reflected from the Earth reaches a sensor on a satellite (4), which transmits the data (5) to a ground station; arrows then lead to analysis and to an application such as maps (6, interpretation and analysis).
blocks.caption: Steps of satellite remote sensing (original diagram after Fig 21.9).
blocks.long_description: The satellite never touches the Earth; it reads the Earth's surface from the sunlight (or other radiation) that the surface reflects or emits.

blocks.prompt: A galaxy is moving away from us very fast. According to Hubble's law, what does that tell us about its distance?
blocks.explanation: It is very far away, since v = Ho d: a larger recession velocity means a larger distance.

blocks.prompt: Using Ho = 2.3 x 10^-18 s^-1, estimate the age of the universe as 1/Ho.
blocks.explanation: 1/Ho = 4.3 x 10^17 s, which is about 1.4 x 10^10 years (14 billion years), close to the accepted 13.8 billion years.

items: Hubble's law v = Ho d; Ho about 2.3 x 10^-18 s^-1.
Balloon model: expansion everywhere, no centre.
Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago; remote sensing in six steps.
